I spoke with a man who said that he didn't think that melting sea ice would raise sea levels.

He tried to explain this to me in terms of the density of the ice and the level at which it floats. He didn't end up writing the math out for me to see, but he proposed an experiment wherein a block of ice is placed in a large beaker, and then the beaker is filled partially with water. We record the height of the water in the beaker and then allow the ice to melt. His hypothesis was that the water level would not rise.

We attempted a similar experiment, but he claimed that the container that we used was bad for the experiment because it allowed the ice to rest on the bottom and the sloped sides of the container, thereby preventing buoyant equilibrium. Also, it was hard to get precise measurements with such a small quantity of ice.

I thought it was an interesting experiment anyway. Some day I hope to replicate it with proper equipment.

But also I realise that in the real world a lot of ice is subject to those same confounding constraints that invalidated the experiment, so his argument doesn't seem very strong to me.
While the ice melting contributes some, the real reason is simpler, heat makes things expand. So the water level would still rise even with no ice in it melting.
The north pole is floating in the water, but all the ice on the south Pole is on land and not subject to that experiment.
